Federal Power. The authority vested in the national government by the United States Constitution, distinguishing it from the reserved powers of states. The Constitution enumerates specific federal powers while allowing implied powers through the Necessary and Proper Clause, creating ongoing tension between centralized and decentralized authority.

The enumerated powers in Article One grant Congress specific, listed authority over coinage, interstate commerce, taxation, national defense, and regulating immigration. The Necessary and Proper Clause, also called the Elastic Clause, permits Congress to pass laws needed to carry out its enumerated powers, vastly expanding federal reach. The Commerce Clause broadly authorizes federal regulation of interstate and foreign commerce, becoming the basis for extensive federal regulatory power covering manufacturing, agriculture, and labor. Marbury v. Madison in eighteen oh-three empowered the Supreme Court to strike down federal laws as unconstitutional, limiting federal power through judicial review and establishing courts as constitutional interpreters. McCulloch v. Maryland in eighteen nineteen affirmed that federal power takes precedence over state power and that implied powers derived from enumerated powers are constitutional and legitimate. The Supremacy Clause establishes that federal law is superior to state law when there is conflict, making federal authority binding on states and individuals. The Tenth Amendment reserves all powers not delegated to the federal government to the states or the people, but courts have read this narrowly, limiting its restraining effect. Federal power expanded dramatically during the Progressive Era and the New Deal, as the Court expanded the Commerce Clause to justify regulation of virtually any economic activity. Federalism—the distribution of power between national and state governments—remains a central and contentious tension in American constitutional law, with battles over healthcare, regulation, and civil rights. Federal power connects to the United States Constitution as the source of all federal power; the Commerce Clause as the basis for broad federal regulatory authority; the Necessary and Proper Clause as the constitutional mechanism for implied powers; McCulloch v. Maryland which affirmed federal supremacy and implied powers; states' rights as the counterbalancing principle limiting federal authority; the Tenth Amendment which reserves unstated powers to the states; and the Supremacy Clause which establishes federal law as supreme over state law.
